titlePl: Matura PR: Państwo i społeczeństwo — 180 haseł do gier LingoSpark
titleEn: Matura Extended: The State and Society — 180 terms for LingoSpark games
blurbPl: Dział Państwo i społeczeństwo na maturę rozszerzoną: ustrój, polityka, prawo, gospodarka i kwestie społeczne. Fiszki ENG–PL.
blurbEn: Extended Matura State and society module: institutions, politics, law, the economy and social issues. ENG–PL flashcards.

items.definitionEn: the basic set of laws that says how a country is governed
items.example: Freedom of assembly is guaranteed in the constitution.

items.definitionEn: the elected body that makes a country's laws
items.example: The new budget must be approved by parliament before April.

items.definitionEn: the councils and officials who run towns, cities and regions
items.example: Bin collections and schools are the responsibility of local government.

items.definitionEn: the system of courts and judges in a country
items.example: An independent judiciary is essential in a democracy.

items.definitionEn: the branch of government that writes and passes laws
items.example: The legislature spent months debating the climate bill.

items.definitionEn: the branch of government that puts laws into practice
items.example: In a parliamentary system, executive power lies mainly with the cabinet.

items.definitionEn: the official who represents a country, such as a president or monarch
items.example: The president is the head of state, while the prime minister leads the government.

items.definitionEn: the group of senior ministers who run government departments
items.example: The cabinet met late into the night before the vote.

items.definitionEn: the professional officials who administer the state, not elected politicians
items.example: A politically neutral civil service should serve any elected government.

items.definitionEn: a person employed by the state to run public administration
items.example: A senior civil servant briefed ministers on the cost of the reform.

items.definitionEn: to approve a proposed law in parliament
items.example: MPs are expected to pass a bill on housing this autumn.

items.definitionEn: a change made to a law or a proposed law
items.example: The opposition tabled an amendment to weaken the surveillance clause.

items.definitionEn: the principle that everyone, including the government, is bound by the law
items.example: Corruption flourishes where the rule of law is weak.

items.definitionEn: dividing state power between legislature, executive and judiciary
items.example: The constitution is based on a clear separation of powers.

items.definitionEn: a system in which citizens choose their leaders in free elections
items.example: A healthy democracy needs an independent press as well as elections.

items.definitionEn: rule by one person or group who hold power by force, not free choice
items.example: In a dictatorship, criticism of the leader can be treated as a crime.

items.definitionEn: a government that demands obedience and limits political freedom
items.example: An authoritarian regime often censors the internet and the press.

items.definitionEn: a system with a king or queen whose powers are limited by law
items.example: The United Kingdom is a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary government.

items.definitionEn: a state whose head is elected or appointed, not a hereditary monarch
items.example: Poland is a republic with a president as head of state.

items.definitionEn: the right of a state to govern itself without outside control
items.example: Joining a treaty can mean sharing a degree of sovereignty with other countries.

items.definitionEn: a district whose voters elect a representative
items.example: Each constituency elects one member of parliament.

items.definitionEn: a person elected to sit in parliament
items.example: Write to your member of parliament if you want the bus route saved.

items.definitionEn: the second chamber of a parliament, such as a senate
items.example: The upper house can delay a bill but not always block it forever.

items.definitionEn: the main elected chamber of a parliament
items.example: Most laws originate in the lower house.

items.definitionEn: a town or district with its own local government
items.example: The municipality opened a new library in the old post office.

items.definitionEn: an elected member of a local council
items.example: A local councillor held a meeting about the planned bypass.

items.definitionEn: a system of administration with many official rules and procedures
items.example: Small firms complain that bureaucracy slows down every permit.

items.definitionEn: official rules that seem unnecessary and delay action
items.example: Teachers say red tape leaves them too little time for actual teaching.

items.definitionEn: a body that monitors institutions and reports abuse
items.example: An independent watchdog organisation published a report on prisons.

items.definitionEn: the organisation and work of government offices and services
items.example: She studied public administration and now works at the regional office.

items.definitionEn: rules that stop any one branch of government becoming too powerful
items.example: A free press is one of the informal checks and balances in a democracy.

items.definitionEn: a law that has been passed by parliament and come into force
items.example: The smoking ban was introduced by an act of parliament.

items.definitionEn: all the people who are entitled to vote
items.example: The party is trying to win back the rural electorate.

items.definitionEn: the percentage of eligible voters who actually vote
items.example: Turnout was highest among older voters and lowest among students.

items.definitionEn: an alliance of parties that govern together
items.example: No party won a majority, so a coalition was formed after weeks of talks.

items.definitionEn: a nationwide vote in which citizens decide a specific question
items.example: The government promised a referendum on the constitutional change.

items.definitionEn: trying to influence politicians and officials on behalf of a group
items.example: Strict rules on lobbying are meant to make politics more transparent.

items.definitionEn: supporting greater social equality and a larger role for the state
items.example: Left-wing parties usually favour higher public spending on welfare.

items.definitionEn: supporting tradition, lower taxes or a smaller role for the state
items.example: Right-wing voters in this region often prioritise law and order.

items.definitionEn: moderate political positions between left and right
items.example: The party moved towards the centre-ground to attract swing voters.

items.definitionEn: a nationwide election to choose a new parliament
items.example: The prime minister called a general election two years early.

items.definitionEn: an electoral system in which seats match the share of votes
items.example: Smaller parties prefer proportional representation to first-past-the-post.

items.definitionEn: a public statement of a party's policies before an election
items.example: The manifesto promised cheaper public transport and more teachers.

items.definitionEn: politics that claims to speak for ordinary people against elites
items.example: Critics say populism oversimplifies complex economic problems.

items.definitionEn: a political belief that puts one's nation first, sometimes at others' expense
items.example: Economic nationalism can lead to higher tariffs on imports.

items.definitionEn: a voter who is not loyal to one party and can decide an election
items.example: The campaign targeted the swing voter in suburban towns.

items.definitionEn: a vote in which nobody can see how you chose
items.example: A secret ballot protects voters from pressure and intimidation.

items.definitionEn: a parliament in which no party has an overall majority
items.example: A hung parliament usually leads to coalition talks.

items.definitionEn: the parties not in government, who criticise those in power
items.example: The opposition accused ministers of hiding the true cost of the plan.

items.definitionEn: a government that does not have a majority of seats
items.example: A minority government must bargain for every vote in parliament.

items.definitionEn: a parliamentary vote to remove the government from office
items.example: The prime minister survived a vote of no confidence by three votes.

items.definitionEn: ordinary members of a party or movement, not its leaders
items.example: The reform began as a grassroots campaign in small towns.

items.definitionEn: the range of political views from left to right
items.example: Most voters place themselves in the middle of the political spectrum.

items.definitionEn: the person or party currently holding office
items.example: The incumbent mayor was defeated after three terms.

items.definitionEn: the right to vote in elections
items.example: Women in Poland gained suffrage in 1918.

items.definitionEn: deprived of the right to vote
items.example: Prisoners in some countries remain disenfranchised until they are released.

items.definitionEn: a survey of people's views, often on parties or policies
items.example: The latest opinion poll put the two main parties neck and neck.

items.definitionEn: an election win by a very large margin
items.example: The party claimed a landslide victory and a clear mandate for reform.

items.definitionEn: to formally decline to vote for or against a motion
items.example: Several rebels decided to abstain rather than vote with the government.

items.definitionEn: illegal interference with the process of an election
items.example: Observers reported possible electoral fraud at two polling stations.

items.definitionEn: the duty of those in power to explain and justify their actions
items.example: A free press is vital for the accountability of public officials.

items.definitionEn: dishonest use of power for private gain, such as taking bribes
items.example: A corruption scandal forced the minister to resign.

items.definitionEn: offering or taking money or gifts to influence an official decision
items.example: The contractor was charged with bribery of a city official.

items.definitionEn: giving jobs or favours to relatives rather than on merit
items.example: Appointing your cousin to the board looks like nepotism.

items.definitionEn: the right to see official documents held by the state
items.example: Journalists used freedom of information requests to check spending.

items.definitionEn: information spread to promote a political cause, often one-sided
items.example: State television was accused of broadcasting propaganda before the vote.

items.definitionEn: to bring a criminal case against someone in court
items.example: Prosecutors decided to prosecute the company for dumping waste.

items.definitionEn: the person accused of a crime or sued in a civil case
items.example: The defendant denied all the charges and pleaded not guilty.

items.definitionEn: unpaid work for the community, given as a punishment
items.example: Instead of a fine, the court ordered 80 hours of community service.

items.definitionEn: relatively minor offences such as shoplifting or vandalism
items.example: The neighbourhood has a problem with petty crime, not with violent gangs.

items.definitionEn: crime planned and carried out by structured groups
items.example: Europol coordinates action against organised crime across the EU.

items.definitionEn: the lawyer who presents the case against the accused
items.example: The prosecutor argued that the evidence left no reasonable doubt.

items.definitionEn: the lawyer who represents the person accused of a crime
items.example: The defence lawyer questioned whether the witness could have seen the incident.

items.definitionEn: a group of citizens who decide if the accused is guilty
items.example: The jury took two days to reach a unanimous verdict.

items.definitionEn: the decision of a jury or court at the end of a trial
items.example: Families waited outside for the verdict to be read.

items.definitionEn: to formally find that someone is not guilty
items.example: The jury voted to acquit her after the key witness changed his story.

items.definitionEn: to find someone guilty of a crime
items.example: It took the jury four hours to convict the two men of fraud.

items.definitionEn: a prison sentence for the rest of a person's life
items.example: The judge imposed life imprisonment for the murder.

items.definitionEn: a sentence served in the community under supervision instead of prison
items.example: He was placed on probation and ordered to attend a rehabilitation course.

items.definitionEn: early release from prison under conditions
items.example: She was granted parole after serving two thirds of the sentence.

items.definitionEn: money paid as a guarantee that an accused person will return to court
items.example: The judge refused bail because the suspect was likely to flee.

items.definitionEn: an official document allowing the police to arrest someone or search a place
items.example: Officers waited for a warrant before they searched the flat.

items.definitionEn: a formal statement given as evidence in court
items.example: Her testimony contradicted the official police report.

items.definitionEn: the principle that a person is innocent until proved guilty
items.example: The presumption of innocence is a cornerstone of a fair trial.

items.definitionEn: a hearing that is independent, public and respects the rights of both sides
items.example: Every defendant has the right to a fair trial, however unpopular they are.

items.definitionEn: a request to a higher court to review a decision
items.example: His lawyers filed an appeal within a week of the sentence.

items.definitionEn: non-violent crime committed by people in business or public office
items.example: Tax fraud is a typical form of white-collar crime.

items.definitionEn: hiding the origin of money obtained from crime
items.example: The bank was fined for failing to stop money laundering.

items.definitionEn: stealing money that you were trusted to look after
items.example: The treasurer was charged with embezzlement of club funds.

items.definitionEn: the illegal trade in people for exploitation
items.example: The police unit specialises in cases of human trafficking.

items.definitionEn: killing someone without the intent required for murder
items.example: He was convicted of manslaughter, not murder, because he had not planned the death.

items.definitionEn: the crime of deliberately setting fire to property
items.example: Investigators treated the warehouse fire as arson.

items.definitionEn: the crime of lying in court after swearing to tell the truth
items.example: She was later charged with perjury over her original statement.

items.definitionEn: helping people who have committed crimes to return to honest life
items.example: The charity focuses on rehabilitation of offenders through training and housing.

items.definitionEn: the tendency of former prisoners to commit further crimes
items.example: Education in prison is one way to reduce recidivism.

items.definitionEn: a serious failure of the legal system, such as convicting an innocent person
items.example: New DNA evidence revealed a miscarriage of justice after twenty years.

items.definitionEn: something that discourages people from committing a crime
items.example: Campaigners doubt that longer sentences are an effective deterrent.

items.definitionEn: the police and other agencies that make sure laws are obeyed
items.example: Cross-border law enforcement is essential against smuggling gangs.

items.definitionEn: a general rise in prices that reduces the value of money
items.example: High inflation has eroded the real value of wages.

items.definitionEn: a period when the economy shrinks for a significant time
items.example: Unemployment usually rises during a recession.

items.definitionEn: the total value of goods and services produced in a country
items.example: Poland's GDP grew faster than the EU average last year.

items.definitionEn: a system in which the state provides healthcare, education and support for those in need
items.example: The welfare state was expanded after the Second World War.

items.definitionEn: illegally hiding income or profits to avoid paying tax
items.example: Offshore accounts were used for tax evasion on a huge scale.

items.definitionEn: using legal loopholes to pay as little tax as possible
items.example: Aggressive tax avoidance by large firms is legal but widely criticised.

items.definitionEn: a tax paid on money you earn from work or investments
items.example: The government raised income tax for the highest earners.

items.definitionEn: money the government spends on services and investment
items.example: Cuts in public spending have hit local libraries and sports centres.

items.definitionEn: the amount by which government spending exceeds income
items.example: A large budget deficit may force the state to borrow more.

items.definitionEn: the total amount a government owes
items.example: Servicing the national debt already takes a slice of every budget.

items.definitionEn: government policy of cutting spending to reduce debt
items.example: Years of austerity left public services understaffed.

items.definitionEn: the percentage of the workforce without a job and seeking one
items.example: The unemployment rate fell to its lowest level in a decade.

items.definitionEn: state help given only if your income is below a limit
items.example: Housing support is a means-tested benefit in many countries.

items.definitionEn: large gaps between what rich and poor people earn
items.example: Income inequality has widened in several European countries.

items.definitionEn: a regular sum paid by the state to every citizen
items.example: Some parties support a trial of universal basic income.

items.definitionEn: money paid by the state to people who have lost their jobs
items.example: She claimed unemployment benefit while looking for a new post.

items.definitionEn: available only if your income and savings are below a set level
items.example: The housing allowance is means-tested, so higher earners do not receive it.

items.definitionEn: selling a state-owned company or service to private owners
items.example: Privatisation of the energy company was deeply unpopular.

items.definitionEn: bringing a private company or sector under state ownership
items.example: The party called for nationalisation of the railways.

items.definitionEn: government cuts in spending to reduce a budget deficit
items.example: Austerity measures closed several community centres in the town.

items.definitionEn: owned and controlled by the government
items.example: The railway remained state-owned after the failed privatisation.

items.definitionEn: money given by the state to keep prices down or support an industry
items.example: Farmers receive a subsidy to keep food production in remote areas.

items.definitionEn: the amount of money needed for basic everyday expenses
items.example: The cost of living crisis has made heating bills a political issue.

items.definitionEn: an increase in the amount of goods and services an economy produces
items.example: Stable economic growth is easier when inflation stays low.

items.definitionEn: illegal trade in goods or currencies that are banned or rationed
items.example: Cigarettes are still sold on the black market to avoid tax.

items.definitionEn: government decisions on tax and public spending
items.example: The budget is the main tool of fiscal policy.

items.definitionEn: how a central bank controls money supply and borrowing costs
items.example: Tight monetary policy is used to slow inflation.

items.definitionEn: not connected with religion; keeping religion out of public institutions
items.example: State schools in Poland are officially secular, even if religion is taught as an optional subject.

items.definitionEn: the state of not having enough money for a decent standard of living
items.example: Child poverty rose when benefits were frozen.

items.definitionEn: an unfair difference in wealth, rights or opportunities
items.example: Income inequality has widened between the capital and smaller towns.

items.definitionEn: unfair treatment of people because of who they are
items.example: Discrimination at work on grounds of age is against the law.

items.definitionEn: the rights of citizens to political and social freedom and equality
items.example: The march was held to defend civil rights and equal treatment before the law.

items.definitionEn: a non-governmental organisation that works independently of the state
items.example: The NGO provides free legal advice to people facing eviction.

items.definitionEn: giving your time unpaid to help other people or a cause
items.example: Volunteering at the food bank taught her more about poverty than any textbook.

items.definitionEn: an organisation that helps people in need; the act of giving that help
items.example: The charity runs shelters and job-training programmes for young people.

items.definitionEn: being shut out of the opportunities most people take for granted
items.example: Long-term unemployment often leads to social exclusion.

items.definitionEn: the ability to move up (or down) the income and class scale
items.example: Affordable higher education is a key driver of social mobility.

items.definitionEn: equal rights and opportunities for women and men
items.example: The report measures gender equality in pay, politics and education.

items.definitionEn: the principle that people should compete on a fair basis, without bias
items.example: The school has an equal opportunities policy for staff recruitment.

items.definitionEn: a crime motivated by hostility towards a person's identity
items.example: The attack was recorded as a hate crime because of the slogans used.

items.definitionEn: dislike or fear of people from other countries
items.example: Politicians were criticised for language that fuelled xenophobia.

items.definitionEn: the sense of solidarity and trust that holds a community together
items.example: Shared public spaces can strengthen social cohesion in mixed neighbourhoods.

items.definitionEn: a situation in which the average age of people in a country is rising
items.example: An ageing population puts pressure on pensions and healthcare.

items.definitionEn: the number of live births per thousand people in a year
items.example: The birth rate has fallen below replacement level.

items.definitionEn: a shift in the size or structure of a population
items.example: Demographic change will shrink the workforce unless immigration rises.

items.definitionEn: the emigration of highly skilled people to other countries
items.example: Low salaries in research have caused a brain drain of young scientists.

items.definitionEn: the difference between the richest and the poorest in a society
items.example: The wealth gap is visible in housing, education and life expectancy.

items.definitionEn: not enjoying the standard of living or rights that most people have
items.example: The scholarship is aimed at underprivileged students from rural schools.

items.definitionEn: pushed to the edge of society and ignored by those in power
items.example: The report looks at how disabled people are still marginalised in the labour market.

items.definitionEn: organisations and citizens acting independently of the state and the market
items.example: A lively civil society can hold governments to account between elections.

items.definitionEn: a faith group that is smaller than the main religion in a country
items.example: The constitution protects every religious minority against discrimination.

items.definitionEn: involving people of different religions working or talking together
items.example: An interfaith forum was set up after tensions in the neighbourhood.

items.definitionEn: citizens taking part in public life, from voting to volunteering
items.example: Schools try to encourage civic engagement through student councils and debates.

items.definitionEn: deliberately breaking a law, peacefully, to protest against it
items.example: The activists chose civil disobedience and blocked the road without violence.

items.definitionEn: a campaign started by ordinary people, not by parties or companies
items.example: A grass-roots movement collected signatures for a local referendum.

items.definitionEn: unity and mutual support among people with a shared goal
items.example: Unions called for solidarity with the striking nurses.

items.definitionEn: the idea that society should be fair in how it shares rights and resources
items.example: The essay asked whether tax policy can promote social justice.

items.definitionEn: giving extra help to a disadvantaged group to make opportunities fairer
items.example: The university's positive discrimination scheme reserves some places for rural applicants.

items.definitionEn: a group of people who regularly worship together
items.example: The congregation collected food and clothes for the shelter.

items.definitionEn: the view that different cultures can live together and keep their identities
items.example: Supporters of multiculturalism argue that diversity strengthens a society.

items.definitionEn: the United Nations, an international organisation for peace and cooperation
items.example: The UN sent observers to monitor the ceasefire.

items.definitionEn: the European Union, a political and economic union of European states
items.example: Poland has been a member of the EU since 2004.

items.definitionEn: a military alliance of North American and European countries
items.example: NATO members are committed to defending one another if one is attacked.

items.definitionEn: food, medicine and shelter given to people in a crisis
items.example: Planes delivered humanitarian aid after the earthquake.

items.definitionEn: penalties, often economic, imposed on a country to change its behaviour
items.example: The EU imposed sanctions on exports of luxury goods.

items.definitionEn: a person who has applied for protection in another country and is waiting for a decision
items.example: An asylum seeker has the right to a fair hearing of their claim.

items.definitionEn: a person who has fled their country because of war or persecution and been granted protection
items.example: A refugee is entitled to international protection under the 1951 Convention.

items.definitionEn: a country that belongs to an international organisation such as the EU
items.example: Each member state sends ministers to meetings of the Council.

items.definitionEn: official political relations between countries
items.example: The two countries restored diplomatic relations after a decade of silence.

items.definitionEn: official help a country gives its citizens abroad
items.example: After the passport was stolen they asked for consular assistance.

items.definitionEn: the senior diplomat who represents a country abroad
items.example: The ambassador was summoned to explain the remarks.

items.definitionEn: international military or civilian operations that help keep a ceasefire
items.example: Polish troops have taken part in UN peacekeeping missions.

items.definitionEn: an agreement to stop fighting for a period of time
items.example: Neither side fully respected the ceasefire overnight.

items.definitionEn: a person who moves to another country mainly to work and improve their living standard
items.example: An economic migrant is not the same as a refugee fleeing persecution.

items.definitionEn: someone forced to leave their home, often still inside their own country
items.example: Camps were set up for every displaced person who fled the fighting.

items.definitionEn: forcing a person to leave a country by official order
items.example: Lawyers are appealing against the deportation of the family.

items.definitionEn: money and expertise given to poorer countries to support long-term progress
items.example: Development aid is meant to build schools and clinics, not only to send food.

items.definitionEn: a country with a lower average income and less industrialised economy
items.example: Debt relief can free money for schools in a developing country.

items.definitionEn: rules that states have agreed should govern relations between them
items.example: The annexation was condemned as a breach of international law.

items.definitionEn: the right to hold, change or practise a faith, or to have none
items.example: Freedom of religion includes the right not to believe.

items.definitionEn: a building or site used for religious practice, such as a church, mosque or synagogue
items.example: The listed barn was converted into a place of worship for the local community.

items.definitionEn: the principle that religious institutions should not run the government, and vice versa
items.example: Supporters of a strict separation of church and state oppose religion lessons in public schools.
